intro: Many real quantities depend on more than one input, like temperature depending on both location and time. This branch learns to picture and handle functions of two or three variables.

VII.10.01.what: A function of several variables takes two or more inputs and gives one output. The domain is the set of inputs that make sense.

levels.a: Reads and evaluates functions written with two inputs, x and y.
levels.b: Finds which input pairs are allowed (the domain).
levels.c: Sketches the domain as a region in the flat plane.

VII.10.02.what: A function of two inputs can be drawn as a surface, like a landscape where the height depends on where you stand.

levels.a: Pictures the graph as a landscape over a flat map.
levels.b: Slices the surface to see cross-section curves (traces).
levels.c: Recognizes common surfaces such as bowls, saddles and cones.
levels.d: Matches surface pictures to their formulas.

VII.10.03.what: Level curves join all points at the same height, exactly like the contour lines on a hiking map.

levels.a: Reads a contour map of a function.
levels.b: Draws level curves for a given function.
levels.c: Reads steepness from how close the contour lines are.
levels.d: Interprets weather maps and topographic maps this way.

VII.10.04.what: For functions of three inputs, points with the same output form surfaces, like shells of equal temperature around a heater.

levels.a: Understands a level surface as all points giving one output.
levels.b: Recognizes spheres and ellipsoids (stretched spheres) as level surfaces.
levels.c: Recognizes other curved surfaces from their equations.
levels.d: Matches level surfaces to their equations.

VII.10.05.what: A limit asks what value a function approaches near a point. With two inputs, you can approach from infinitely many directions.

levels.a: Sees that a point can be approached along many different paths.
levels.b: Shows a limit does not exist by finding two paths that disagree.
levels.c: Switches to distance-and-angle coordinates to find a limit.
levels.d: Traps a function between two simpler ones to find its limit.

VII.10.06.what: A function is continuous where it has no sudden jumps or holes, so small moves in the inputs give small changes in the output.

levels.a: Understands the definition of continuity with two inputs.
levels.b: Knows sums, products and compositions of continuous functions stay continuous.
levels.c: Finds where a given function is continuous.
levels.d: Fills in a single missing point to remove a break.
